title: Valid Parentheses
description: Validate balanced brackets with a stack, and extend it to wildcard and minimum-addition variants.

data.text: Given a string containing only `(`, `)`, `{`, `}`, `[`, and `]`, determine whether the brackets are balanced: every opening bracket is closed by the matching type, and brackets close in the correct order.
Repeatedly remove the substrings `()`, `[]`, and `{}` until none remain. If the string is empty, it was balanced. Correct, but O(n²) and allocation-heavy.

data.title: Replacement O(n²)
data.content: Peel off inner pairs until nothing changes.

data.text: Push every opening bracket. On a closing bracket, the top of the stack must be its matching opener — anything else is invalid. At the end the stack must be empty, otherwise some bracket was never closed.

data.title: Stack O(n)
data.content: One pass, one stack, two failure conditions.

data.title: Two ways to fail, and both must be checked
data.text: Unbalanced brackets fail either by a mismatched pair (`(]`) or by leaving openers on the stack (`((`). Handling only the mismatch check and forgetting `stack.Count == 0` is the most common incomplete answer.

data.title: A cleaner matching rule
data.text: Instead of pushing openers and comparing types, push the **expected closer** for each opener. On a closing bracket, simply check `stack.Pop() == c`. This removes the three-way comparison and reads better.

If `*` can mean `(`, `)`, or nothing, a single stack is not enough. Track the range of possible open-bracket counts with two counters — the fewest and the most open brackets the string could currently have.

data.title: Wildcard variant with a count range
data.content: Maintain low and high possible depths instead of an exact stack.

data.caption: Opening brackets are pushed; each closing bracket must pop its matching opener, and the stack must end empty.
data.definition:
graph TD
    A["s = ([{}])"] --> B["push ( -> [(]"]
    B --> C["push [ -> [(,[]"]
    C --> D["push { -> [(,[,{]"]
    D --> E["} pops { - match"]
    E --> F["] pops [ - match"]
    F --> G[") pops ( - match, stack empty -> true"]
    style G fill:#e8f5e9,stroke:#2e7d32

cards.title: Replacement
cons: Allocates a new string each round

data.title: Complete solution
data.content: The stack version of bracket matching is the same mechanism compilers use to parse nested syntax, and the same idea detects malformed HTML and validates string templates. Learning the expected-closer trick makes the code much shorter.
